plan.topic: Tirzepatide switched on calorie-burning brown fat, but only in obese mice
plan.angle: 'Does Mounjaro speed up your metabolism?' In obese mice, tirzepatide switched brown fat back on. Put 'in mice' on screen. In people there's only an early, small signal from a conference study, and it's not proven to raise calorie burn in a meaningful way. Explain brown fat in one line and why mouse results often don't carry over (adults have much less brown fat). Then what human trials do show: lower appetite and 'food noise', and better blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Add a talk-to-your-doctor line.
plan.working_title: Does Mounjaro Speed Up Your Metabolism? What the Mouse Study Actually Showed #shorts
plan.why: Myth-busting slot. Overhyped headlines ran Sep 26–27, momentum is climbing, and it fits the 'how GLP-1 works' pillar. | fact-check: The mouse studies exist (ScienceDaily, September 2026; Life Sciences 2025/PubMed 41412277, which used estrogen-deficient obese diabetic mice). But 'not shown in humans' is too absolute. At ENDO 2026, an Endocrine Society press release on a human study described a 'signal consistent with' brown fat activation after tirzepatide. That is early and preliminary, but it exists. Per the craft notes, avoid absolute claims.

social.instagram_caption:
Mounjaro = faster metabolism? Not quite. 🔬

Here's what the studies actually found:

• In estrogen-deficient, obese, diabetic mice, tirzepatide (the drug in Mounjaro) showed signs of switching brown fat back on. Brown fat burns calories for heat.
• Mice rely on brown fat way more than we do, so this doesn't automatically carry over to people.
• In one small trial of 34 women with obesity (presented at a conference, not yet published), brown fat activity looked higher on scans — but resting calorie burn did NOT go up.
• What human trials do show in people with type 2 diabetes: tirzepatide lowers appetite, reduces food intake, and improves blood sugar.

So the honest answer: not a proven "faster engine" in humans. Think quieter appetite, not a metabolic boost.

Save this for the next time a headline claims a GLP-1 "speeds up your metabolism" 📌

factcheck.summary: The script is accurate, well-framed and safe. The mouse study (src1) is real: it's in Life Sciences, with ovariectomized mice that had obesity and type 2 diabetes. In those mice, tirzepatide reversed brown fat whitening and restored thermogenic markers such as UCP1. The script clearly labels this as a mouse result. The human data (TABFAT, src4/src7) is described correctly: 34 women with obesity in a 24-week RCT presented at ENDO 2026, June 2026. Brown fat activity on PET/CT rose from 41.2% to 64.7% of participants on tirzepatide. Resting energy expenditure didn't differ between groups, and it fell numerically more on tirzepatide. So "didn't go up" is correct. I found no full peer-reviewed publication of TABFAT; the 2025 Trials paper describes the design only. The ScienceDaily piece from September 2026 is a separate mouse study, not TABFAT. Heise 2023 in Diabetes Care (reduced appetite, energy intake and fat mass in type 2 diabetes) and SURPASS-2 (glucose control) back up scene s6. The review papers (JCI 2015, Sidossis & Kajimura) and Cypess (NEJM 2009) support what the script says about brown fat. The script keeps correlation separate from causation and mice separate from humans. It avoids claims about dosing, includes a talk-to-your-doctor CTA, and the hook delivers on what it promises. Only minor fixes are listed.

issues.problem: PubMed lists src1 in Life Sciences volume 386 (2026). It was published online in late 2025. The source list should give the issue year.
issues.fix: Change src1 year to "2026" (keep the same title and URL).

issues.problem: No full paper turned up as of September 2026, but a flat 'not yet published' could go out of date or be wrong. This follows the craft rule to hedge absolute claims. Also, all participants were premenopausal, which narrows who the result applies to.
issues.fix: In people? One small trial in thirty-four premenopausal women with obesity, presented at a conference and not yet published in full, saw more brown fat activity on scans. That's early. And in that same trial, resting calorie burn didn't go up.
